title: Dependencies, SBOMs and pinned actions
summary: Know what you ship, find the vulnerable parts, and stop third-party code changing under you.

steps.title: Your dependencies are your code
body: A typical .NET API ships a few thousand lines of yours and hundreds of thousands from NuGet packages. A vulnerability in any of them is
a vulnerability in your app.
```text
dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive
Project 'Api'
Transitive Package          Resolved   Severity   Advisory URL
> System.Text.Json          8.0.0      High       https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-...
- **Transitive** dependencies (dependencies of dependencies) are the majority, so always include them.
- Run the scan **in CI on every PR** and on a **schedule**: new advisories appear for code you have not touched.
- Tools like Dependabot open PRs that bump vulnerable versions; your test suite is what makes merging them safe.

steps.prompt: Nobody changed the repo for three months, yet the nightly pipeline started failing its vulnerability gate. Why?
options: A new advisory was published for a package version you already use
steps.explain: Vulnerability data changes daily. That is why scans run on a schedule, not only on code changes.

steps.title: SBOM
body: A **Software Bill of Materials** lists every component in a build: name, version, licence, and a package URL such as
`pkg:nuget/Newtonsoft.Json@13.0.3`. Standard formats are **CycloneDX** and **SPDX**.
Why bother: when the next Log4Shell-style vulnerability is announced, "which of our 200 services ship `X` below version `Y`?" becomes a
query over SBOMs instead of a week of archaeology. Generate it in the pipeline and attach it to the release artifact.

steps.prompt: Match each supply-chain tool to its job.
pairs: machine-readable list of what a build contains
catch credentials pushed to the repo
find dangerous patterns in your own code

steps.title: Pin your actions
body: `uses: some-org/deploy-action@v2` runs whatever commit the tag `v2` points to **today**. If that repo is compromised, the attacker moves
the tag and your next run executes their code with your secrets. This has happened (e.g. the `tj-actions/changed-files` incident in 2025).
```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v7                                        # tag: can move
- uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683  # v4.2.2 - full SHA: cannot move
Pin third-party actions to a **full 40-character commit SHA** (keep the version in a comment; Dependabot can update both).
Local actions (`uses: ./.github/actions/setup`) live in your own repo and need no pin.

steps.prompt: Is the reference pinned to an immutable commit?
A scan compares installed versions with the first fixed version. Which packages are reported, one per line?
steps.explain: `13.0.1` is the fixed version itself, so Newtonsoft.Json is safe; Serilog has no advisory.

steps.prompt: Order the response to a critical advisory in a dependency.
lines: Scheduled scan flags the vulnerable version
Check whether the vulnerable code path is reachable
Bump the package and run the full pipeline
Confirm the new SBOM shows the fixed version
steps.explain: Even when the path is unreachable, bumping is usually cheapest; the check decides the urgency.

steps.title: Find vulnerable dependencies
prompt: Write `List<string> Vulnerable(Dictionary<string, string> installed, List<(string Package, string FixedIn)> advisories)`.
A package is vulnerable when it is installed at a version **older** than `FixedIn` (plain `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, compared numerically).
Return lines like `"System.Text.Json 8.0.4 -> 8.0.5"`, sorted ordinally, without duplicates. A helper method `IsOlder` is a good idea.
starter: List<string> Vulnerable(Dictionary<string, string> installed, List<(string Package, string FixedIn)> advisories)
solution: List<string> Vulnerable(Dictionary<string, string> installed, List<(string Package, string FixedIn)> advisories)
.Where(a => installed.TryGetValue(a.Package, out var v) && IsOlder(v, a.FixedIn))
hints: `installed.TryGetValue(pkg, out var v)` skips packages you do not use.
Compare the three numbers in turn; equal versions are not older.
template: Dojo.Eq("numeric comparison", new List<string> { "Serilog 3.1.0 -> 3.10.0" }, Vulnerable(dojoInstalled, new() { ("Serilog", "3.10.0") }));
Dojo.Eq("not installed", new List<string>(), Vulnerable(dojoInstalled, new() { ("Log4Net", "2.0.10") }));
